evidence: Quote found verbatim: design/manuscript/chapter-09/chapter-09.md L34 'bandwidth drops ~2 orders of magnitude from HBM to the cluster fabric — the reason the interconnect, not the GPU, often binds at scale'. Table 9-1 rows read at L28 (HBM3 3.35 TB/s) and L31/L32 (RoCE ~50 GB/s per port; IB 25/50 GB/s per port). Recomputed: 3350/50 = 67x (log10 = 1.83); 3350/25 = 134x (log10 = 2.13) — both round to ~2 under the caption's explicit '~' approximation, and the causal clause is qualified with 'often'. The finding itself concedes defensibility; no arithmetic error exists in the source.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L18 'Used when a model split across nodes needs the full weight or KV cache locally.' The statement is conditional ('Used when...needs'), not a claim of normal practice. The weight half is book-endorsed: chapter-09.md L192 describes 'FSDP-style weight gathering ... does all-gather weight shards before the forward pass'. The same line explicitly rules out routine full-tensor gathering: 'weight matrices stay resident and are read in place, they are not re-fetched each step' and KV moves as a one-time fragment. The chapter therefore never establishes a 'normally all-gathered KV' path; residual issue is only that the KV example is uncommon.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L116 'why model parallelism and pipeline parallelism exist'. The book itself uses model parallelism as the umbrella elsewhere: chapter-09.md L150 'We might choose model parallelism (pipeline parallelism, tensor parallelism)' — so L116 coordinates the genus with one of its species as if they were alternative categories. Terminology drift between the two lines is real and internal to the source.
fix_instruction: chapter-09.md L116: replace 'why model parallelism and pipeline parallelism exist' with 'why tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism exist' (or 'why model-parallel strategies such as tensor and pipeline parallelism exist'), matching the umbrella usage already used at L150.

evidence: Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L116 'against the savings from fitting a larger model'. The worked example computes communication time only — chapter-09.md L114: 'These totals exclude overlap and computation'. No memory-saving term is defined, but the sentence is a qualitative instruction ('budget the extra seconds ... against the savings'), not a claim of a computed comparison; 'savings' reads as the enabling benefit versus not fitting the model at all. Style-level phrasing, no factual error.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L136 'PCIe Gen5 x16 peaks at ~64 GB/s, but a single all-reduce usually does not saturate the full link: ... so one link rarely carries the whole transfer.' The same line's own parenthetical undercuts it: 'by the ring model of §9.3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor' — for N=8 that is 7/8 = 87.5%, i.e. nearly the whole transfer, so 'rarely carries the whole transfer' cannot explain sub-peak effective bandwidth (40–60% per the same line). Saturation depends on rate, not on whether one link carries 100%; the stated reason is a non sequitur contradicted by the line's own (N−1)/N figure.
fix_instruction: chapter-09.md L136: rewrite the bullet so sub-peak effective bandwidth is attributed to protocol overhead, latency, message size and contention; state per-link ring volume as (N−1)/N per phase (7/8 for N=8) and do not use 'traffic is split across links / one link rarely carries the whole transfer' as the explanation for unsaturation.

evidence: Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L136 'and by the ring model of §9.3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor.' §9.3 states the scope the parenthetical omits — chapter-09.md L90: 'Each phase sends (N-1)M/N=122.5 GB per rank; reduce-scatter followed by all-gather therefore sends 245 GB' — so per-link total is 2(N−1)/N (245 GB = 2x122.5 for N=8, M=140). For N=2 the unqualified parenthetical reads 1/2 while total per-link traffic is one full tensor, which is what the preceding clause ('A two-rank collective over one path ... can saturate the link') relies on. The factor of 2 and the per-phase qualifier are genuinely absent from the parenthetical.
fix_instruction: chapter-09.md L136: change the parenthetical to 'per phase each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor; over the full reduce-scatter plus all-gather each link carries 2(N−1)/N — for N=2 that totals one full tensor per link, which is why a two-rank collective can saturate the link.'

evidence: Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L136 '(the §9.3 worked example's 40 GB/s and 2.5 GB/s are optimistic ~80% upper bounds — label them as such)'. The antecedent IS named inline ('the §9.3 worked example's'), and §9.3 states the links: chapter-09.md L100 'HDR InfiniBand delivers 200 Gb/s per link (≈ 25 GB/s ... ) ... A realistic effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node)' -> 2 rails x 25 = 50 GB/s aggregate, 40/50 = 0.80; L108 '25 Gb/s ≈ 3.125 GB/s ... practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s' -> 2.5/3.125 = 0.80. Both ~80% figures recompute against the links the parenthetical cites; the finding's 40/64 = 62.5% path requires ignoring the explicit '§9.3' attribution. The finding's own evidence concedes 40/50 = 0.80 and 2.5/3.125 = 0.80.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L138 'spent exclusively in communication'. The finding's core evidence claim — 'The text does not state the overlap assumption' — is contradicted by the same bullet and its cited section: L138 itself says '(a flat lower bound; ~98 s with the ring factor, §9.3)', and chapter-09.md L114 (§9.3) states explicitly 'These totals exclude overlap and computation; they do not predict a real training iteration without its collective schedule.' The phrase describes the nature of the cumulative 56,000 s (collective duration), which remains 56,000 s whether or not it is overlapped; the no-overlap scope is stated in the cited section.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L148 'keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 1/11th the assumed InfiniBand case ... (§9.3)'. The ratio recomputes from the directly cited section: §9.3 L100 states the assumed IB effective bandwidth ('A realistic effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node)'), L103 gives T_ring ≈ 6.1 s, L98 gives the ideal NVLink ring ≈ 0.54 s (245/450), and L114 states 'the InfiniBand time is about 11x the ideal NVLink ring time' — 6.1/0.54 ≈ 11.3, equivalently 450/40 = 11.25. The finding's acceptance test (recomputes from a named rate in the same paragraph or a directly cited section) is satisfied; the HDR-25-GB/s figure at L142 is a per-port line rate, while §9.3's 40 GB/s is the multi-rail effective figure the ratio uses, and L148 further labels the ratios 'peak-vs-effective upper bounds'.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L192 'the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs, at the canonical batch and hidden size — it scales with batch x hidden width per layer)'. The sentence's own frame is per-STEP movement, and the tens-of-MBs figure recomputes as the per-step aggregate: the book's own worked example (chapter-10.md L~175 area: '16 active sequences ... hidden width 8,192, two-byte BF16 ... two output all-reduces per transformer block ... 80 blocks') gives 16 x 8192 x 2 B x 2 x 80 ≈ 42 MB per step; at the canonical ~17.5-concurrent point ≈ 46 MB. Per-layer volume is 0.03–0.5 MB, so the finding's 'wrong' claim holds only under the per-layer reading the sentence's 'per-step data movement' frame does not support. Residual ambiguity between per-layer and per-step is real, but the number itself is correct under the source's own framing.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L136 'PCIe Gen5 x16 peaks at ~64 GB/s' — no direction qualifier in the bullet. The manuscript is direction-qualified everywhere else: chapter-09.md L30 (Table 9-1) '~64 GB/s per x16 direction', and L29 labels NVLink 'bidirectional aggregate'. A reader comparing the unqualified bullet figure against bidirectional aggregates (e.g. NVLink 900 GB/s bidirectional) can compute the wrong ratio; the missing qualifier is verifiable in the current source.
fix_instruction: chapter-09.md L136: change to 'PCIe Gen5 x16 peaks at ~64 GB/s per direction (~128 GB/s bidirectional aggregate)', matching the Table 9-1 wording at L30.

evidence: Quote found verbatim: chapter-09.md L138 'A 70B model gradient all-reduce at 25 Gb/s Ethernet'. The bullet indeed omits precision, but it cites §9.3 in the same sentence ('~98 s with the ring factor, §9.3') and §9.3 states the assumption explicitly: chapter-09.md L90 'a 70B model has 140 GB of FP16 weights. We separately assume an FP16 gradient tensor of logical size M=140 GB at each rank.' The bullet's numbers derive from that cited example (140/2.5 = 56), so the precision is one inline cross-reference away, not absent from the source.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-10.md L5 'the five parallelization strategies — tensor, pipeline, data, expert, and sequence parallelism — plus a serving-only sixth (P/D disaggregation, which has no training counterpart)'. The claimed misclassification does not hold: chapter-10.md L9 states the framing 'splitting one of the three things a model occupies — its weights, its layers, or its data' (data splitting is an endorsed category, so DP is not misfiled as model partitioning) and defines P/D as 'splitting the prefill stage from the decode stage into separate pools'; L13-L19 label each strategy's split (TP splits a layer's weights, PP splits layers, DP 'replicates all weights ... feeds each a different batch', EP shards experts). Data parallelism is standardly called a parallelization strategy, and P/D is explicitly flagged serving-only in the quoted clause itself. The finding's own acceptance test (each item labels what is split/replicated; no item misclassified) is already met by the source.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-10.md L5 'a single GPU cannot hold this model or keep up with this workload'. Under standard English 'cannot A or B' means unable to do either — it already covers failing one constraint or both; the finding's reading of two 'mutually exclusive failure modes' has no textual basis (no exclusivity marker exists in the sentence), and the proposed fix ('cannot hold, cannot keep up, or both') adds no logical content. The chapter later treats the constraints separately (L9 'weight-residency, the workload's batch shape'), which is compatible with the sentence as written.

Both fragments found in chapter-11.md: L48 'TTFT budget 1.2 s, TPOT ~25 ms/token' and L54 'inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach'. The finding's claim that the second SLO is undefined fails: chapter-11.md L130 states 'near-mandatory to hold TTFT under the SLO (1.2 s, p95 <= 2 s)' — both thresholds defined and distinguished — and L223 'p95 TTFT of 2.2 s against a 2 s SLO'. The same convention appears book-wide: chapter-08.md L299 'p95 TTFT is 2.8 s, exceeding the 2 s p95 TTFT SLO (the 1.2 s figure is the internal design budget)'. There is no stale or undefined value: 1.2 s = design budget, 2 s = p95 SLO, both explicitly stated.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-11.md L68 'PagedAttention/vLLM allocates KV in fixed blocks shared and evicted like page frames, so the ~24.9 GB per request is packed densely'. The sentence attributes block SHARING to PagedAttention's allocation mechanism, but its own stated benefit is packing density, not sharing; sharing is a copy-on-write/prefix-reuse feature, and the chapter attributes prefix dedup to prefix caching separately — chapter-11.md L98 'prefix caching instead dedupes shared prefixes (prefix-hit rate) — track the two separately'. The word 'shared' therefore blurs the mechanism the same chapter keeps distinguishable.
fix_instruction: chapter-11.md L68: replace 'allocates KV in fixed blocks shared and evicted like page frames' with 'allocates KV in fixed-size blocks mapped through a per-request block table and evicted like page frames; blocks are shared across requests only when the engine implements copy-on-write or prefix reuse'.

evidence: Quote found verbatim: chapter-11.md L22 'These mechanisms compose: continuous batching is the baseline, PagedAttention makes it memory-efficient, prefix caching makes it cheaper, and P/D disaggregation makes it scale.' The sentence is a four-part parallel summary of mechanism roles, and the chapter explicitly states the condition two sections later — chapter-11.md L~130: 'For the canonical single-host (~10 rps) this disaggregation is premature; it pays off when measured prefill/decode interference binds — evaluate it against measured phase conflict, not topology alone'. The conditional the finding asks for already exists in the source; the summary line is genre-appropriate compression, not an unreconciled universal claim.

Both formulations found in chapter-11.md (first broken only by markdown emphasis): L20 'reports up to **525% throughput lift** in long-context simulation and **75% more requests** than the paper's baseline method' and later in §3 'Mooncake's reported up to 525% long-context throughput (a lift over the paper's own baseline configuration, from its long-context simulation results)'. The two phrasings differ ('throughput lift' vs bare 'throughput') and neither states the multiplier: '525% lift' reads as 6.25x baseline while '525% throughput' reads as 5.25x baseline; the parenthetical 'a lift over the paper's own baseline configuration' still does not resolve which. A third mention (L217 'Mooncake's 525%/75%') is likewise bare.
fix_instruction: chapter-11.md: in both locations state the baseline and multiplier explicitly (e.g. 'up to 525% higher long-context throughput (6.25x the paper's own baseline)' or '5.25x baseline', whichever matches Mooncake [S4]) and use the identical formulation in L20, the §3 sentence, and L217.

evidence: Quote found (normalized) at chapter-11.md L98: 'Measure KV utilization — fraction of the 640 GB node memory consumed by live KV vs weights. PagedAttention raises effective KV packing (block utilization); prefix caching instead dedupes shared prefixes (prefix-hit rate) — track the two separately.' The definition is explicit and unambiguous (the reader knows exactly what to measure), the node-memory breakdown is a legitimate measurement, and the item already names the capacity-denominator metric separately as 'block utilization' plus 'prefix-hit rate'. The issue is a naming collision with the industry's KV-cache-utilization metric (used KV / KV capacity), not an executable error — the finding's evidence that the item 'presumes a KV-capacity denominator' is inaccurate, since the item gives the node-memory denominator explicitly and labels the capacity metric separately.

Quote found verbatim: chapter-11.md L108 'Requests that exit at different iterations can leave an initially uniform batch with different amounts of remaining computation.' The immediately preceding sentence in the same paragraph defines the unit as token-level: 'Adaptive depth (per-token early exit — the same early-exit interface above) changes the scheduler's unit of work.' The next sentence then attributes exit to requests, contradicting the per-token definition it builds on; L106 also defines the interface as 'a trained head that lets a token leave before the final layer'. The unit-of-work confusion is internal to the source.
fix_instruction: chapter-11.md L108: replace 'Requests that exit at different iterations' with 'Tokens that exit at different iterations' (and state that a request may contain a mix of exit depths, so its remaining computation per sequence differs).
